title: Cut-through switches
text: Every switch between you and the exchange adds delay. How much depends on when it starts sending the frame on.

title: Store and forward
text: A store-and-forward switch takes in the whole frame, checks it, and only then sends it out. So every hop adds at least the time to clock the frame in. At 10 gigabits per second, a 64 byte frame takes about 51 nanoseconds, and a 1,518 byte frame about 1.2 microseconds.

title: Cut-through
text: A cut-through switch starts sending once it has read the destination address, in the first few bytes. The front of the frame leaves while its tail is still arriving, so the delay no longer grows with frame size. The catch is the checksum, which comes last. By the time it fails, the bad frame is already on its way. And if the output port is busy, or slower than the input, the switch has to buffer anyway.

title: Vendor figures
text: Vendor datasheets give the scale. Cisco quotes its Nexus 3548 at latencies as low as 250 nanoseconds, or 200 in its warp mode, and 50 for Warp SPAN, which copies one input to several outputs. Arista quotes 5 nanoseconds for layer 1 switching in its 7130 series, the same as one metre of fibre. Layer 1 devices patch, tap and replicate ports, rather than switching frames by address.

title: A hop budget
text: Now add up a path with three switches and 30 metres of fibre, for a full-size frame at 10 gigabits. Fibre adds about 150 nanoseconds. Three store-and-forward hops add 3.6 microseconds of clocking in alone. Three cut-through hops at 250 nanoseconds add 0.75. The switch choice outweighs the cable. Thirty metres of fibre costs less than a single store-and-forward hop.

title: Queues beat everything
text: The bigger enemy is queueing. When two inputs send to one output at the same moment, one frame waits for the other. One full-size frame ahead of yours costs 1.2 microseconds, more than a whole cut-through hop. Bursts at the open fill these queues fast.

title: In the lab
text: The lab's feed caps each MoldUDP64 packet, header included, at 1,400 bytes by default, so with UDP and IP headers it fits a 1,500 byte MTU. On a real 10 gigabit link, that keeps each frame's clocking time under 1.2 microseconds. The lab itself runs on loopback, with no switch in the path, so use this video's numbers to budget a real one.

title: Takeaway
text: Count hops, keep frames small, and watch the queues. That is where the nanoseconds go. Next, the longest hop of all: Chicago to New Jersey.
